articles.title_orig: Stock futures mixed after Nasdaq correction; Japan's Nikkei 225 enters bear market: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures mixed after Nasdaq correction; Japan's Nikkei 225 enters bear market: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures were mixed early Friday after a punishing sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks that sent the Nasdaq into correction territory. Traders also awaited a key payrolls report.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average slumped 1.3%. S&P 500 futures were down 0.35%, while Nasdaq-100 futures inched 0.3% higher, clawing back a fraction of heavy losses suffered on Thursday.
In Asia, South Korea led losses in the region, with the Kospi plunging more than 6%. Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 5.9%, falling into bear market territory. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.9%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 1%, and mainland China's CSI 300 declined 1.47%.
The moves follow a bout of heavy selling during Thursday's regular Wall Street session that saw the three major averages post their worst one-day performances since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite tanked 5.5%, closing more than 10% below its most recent high and landing in correction territory. The broad-market S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%.
While all 11 sectors of the S&P 500 closed with losses, shares of companies tied to the AI build-out suffered keenly. Democrats' big wins in the House and Senate, as well as key governorships in states like Texas, sparked traders' worries of a potential slowdown in data center construction.
Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices plummeted 17% each, while neocloud CoreWeave slid 10%. Even the Magnificent Seven weren't spared, as Nvidia dropped 9%, turning negative for 2026, and the cohort of tech juggernauts shed more than $1 trillion in aggregate market cap.
The three major averages are poised for losses on the week, with the Nasdaq down 4.4% and the S&P 500 off almost 3% in the period. The 30-stock Dow is the relative outperformer of the three, off just 0.5% week to date.
The pullback creates a buying opportunity, Victoria Greene, CIO at G Squared Private Wealth told CNBC Thursday. "The AI trade, in my opinion, is not dead here," she said, adding, "it's a good discount." She's interested in memory stocks, citing how management teams throughout this earnings season have been talking about the capacity crunch. "Buying a volatile dip tends to be good as long as we're still in a non-recessionary period," she said.
Another market catalyst awaits investors on Friday morning in the form of the October payrolls report. The Dow Jones consensus estimate is for 59,000 jobs added last month and for the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.2%.
Correction: Victoria Greene is the CIO of G Squared Private Wealth. An earlier version misspelled her name.
The sharp sell-off in AI-related names this week reflects an adjustment in growth expectations to a more sustainable level, according to William de Gale, co-founder and lead portfolio manager at Blue Box Asset Management — but it does not change "insatiable" levels of demand.
De Gale told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" that the technology sector had been delivering consistent profits and stock price growth of around 15% for nearly two decades. This was connected to a host of supply constraints, including in semiconductor equipment, raw materials, energy, staffing and permitting, which cap the growth rate, he said.
"AI has been able to grow a lot faster than that in recent years because it's been a lot smaller. It's a subset of the tech sector by and large, but eventually it becomes big enough that it runs into that overall constraint, and I think that's really what's happening now," de Gale said.
"The industry seems to be ahead of what expectations are, ahead of what is sustainable, and at the moment, all the models have 30% top line growth in them, going many years into the future, and nothing that big can grow that fast very long, so those models all need to come down to 15, to 20%, and that's the adjustment that's happening at the moment."
"I don't think there's any real issue with demand. The demand is insatiable, and the demand outside AI is pretty much insatiable as well."
Asia-Pacific markets tumbled on Friday, as a sharp sell-off in technology stocks swept across the region.
South Korea's Kospi fell more than 6%, leading losses in the region to end at 5,059.69, and declining 11.7% this week. The small-cap, tech-focused Kosdaq fell 5.03%, closing at 644.27.
Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 5.96% to 57,434.77, entering bear market territory.
Mainland China's CSI 300 fell 1.44% lower at 4,054.28, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng was down 1.32% as of its last hour of trade.
Taiwan's Taiex also entered bear market, dropping 4.51% to 39,701.64. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.49% at 9,020.8.
Germany's Daimler Truck reported an 89% year-on-year increase in earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to 1.05 billion euros ($1.18 billion).
North American truck sales jumped 51%, which the company attributed to both a continued market recovery and the impact of tariff uncertainty in the same quarter last year. The North American market for heavy-duty trucks fell 7% in the first three quarters, but was offset by 8% growth in Europe.
Daimler, one of the world's biggest truck manufacturers, flagged ongoing market challenges, including slowing growth, rising energy costs and uncertainty in the global economy.
CFO Eva Scherer said the company showed "discipline in converting performance into cash" in the quarter and was "determined to maintain that discipline."
The U.S. is likely to resume military action against Iran in the coming days, a move that could send oil prices sharply higher, according to Bob McNally, CEO at geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group.
Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," McNally put the odds of "a resumption of military fighting" at 80% as the U.S. midterm elections recede.
McNally said he expects both Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures to rise above $100 a barrel. The benchmarks are currently trading at about $100 and $91, respectively.
"President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added.
Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector.

Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.

articles.title_orig: New anti-corruption law arms Beijing with expansive global enforcement powers
articles.title_zh: New anti-corruption law arms Beijing with expansive global enforcement powers
articles.content_orig:
Authorities can now probe Chinese firms’ misconduct in any jurisdiction, while blocking unauthorised foreign investigations
The Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law was approved at the close of the 25th session of the 14th National People’s Congress Standing Committee (NPCSC) and took effect immediately, according to the state news agency Xinhua.
The statute establishes formal mechanisms for handling cross-border cases, international cooperation and asset recovery.

articles.title_orig: China's Macau jails ex-lawmaker in first national security trial
articles.title_zh: China's Macau jails ex-lawmaker in first national security trial
articles.content_orig:
Au was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state"
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail . Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

articles.title_orig: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.title_zh: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.content_orig:
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.
“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).
Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran , which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?
It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.
“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.
Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.
“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.
“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.
By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.
“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.
Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.
Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.
Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.
“India and Qatar have closer relationships with DC they need to maintain – while both of them also feel let down by Trump,” Parsi said, adding, “For Qatar, maintaining a relationship with Iran is also vital since it’s an unavoidable neighbour.”
“So for all of them, there are upsides for these exemptions from Iranian restrictions but also political dangers,” he said.
Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.
With the Iraqi exemption, Iran “probably intends to support the economic recovery” of its western neighbour, a fellow Shia-majority country, Pusztai said.
That depends on Washington.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.
It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.
But Hayat Moqaddam did not appear to limit the exemptions to ships trading with other Gulf states, Pusztai noted. “If this is really the case, this would also have a significant impact on the other Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“This could make the continuation of the American naval blockade more difficult and less effective, assuming Washington accepts this Iranian move,” he said. The main change, he added, is that the exemption “would also cover Chinese/Indian ships from/to Iran”, if the US accepts it.
It is also unclear whether “ships of these countries” means the flag a vessel flies, its owner, its operator or some other link, Pusztai said.
Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.
“It seems to be that Iran tries to separate the questions of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and oil exports from the nuclear question,” Pusztai said, adding, “The American reaction will show if this is successful.”
“I think they make only limited difference at present,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
“Markets are back to pricing in a peace deal, but if conflict flares up at full tilt, then Iranian commanders may not have time to distinguish their targets,” he said, adding: “At present, the focus remains squarely on the prospects of a broader deal.”
An exemption has not guaranteed safety. On October 30, the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Gulf, said its owner, Qatar Gas Transport Company.
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

articles.title_orig: Asian Stocks Brace for Selloff as AI Rout Deepens: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks Brace for Selloff as AI Rout Deepens: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector.
The rout came as investors worried that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure.
In Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2%, while Tokyo Electron slid 7.3%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 11.6%.
Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.
In Taiwan, semiconductor stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with contract chipmaker TSMC sliding 9.6%. Electronics manufacturers Hon Hai Precision Industry , also known as Foxconn, and Foxconn Technology fell 9.4% and 9.1%, respectively, as the regional technology rout deepened.
China was also caught in the regional sell-off, with the tech-heavy STAR Market and the ChiNext Artificial Intelligence Index both tumbling more than 4%.
The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending. It closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%.
The sell-off in Asian equities has been exacerbated by investors unwinding positions, stop-loss selling and heightened volatility, Timothy Moe, chief Asia Pacific equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Friday. He added that potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect demand and profits for Asian AI hardware suppliers.
"If there's concern about the speed and magnitude of buildout in the U.S., then obviously that's going to put all that into question," he said. "The market's tendency is always to shoot first and ask questions later. I think that's exactly what's happening now."

articles.title_orig: 12 Planes in 12 Days: Pope Begins Major Latin America Tour, Weeks After Surgery
articles.title_zh: 12 Planes in 12 Days: Pope Begins Major Latin America Tour, Weeks After Surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title_orig: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 5, 2026
articles.title_zh: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 5, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
The Kremlin is weaponizing humanitarian crises Russia itself has created in order to court the Trump Administration. The White House reported on November 5 that First Lady Melania Trump hosted Ukrainian and Russian officials in recognition of the success of the recent limited ceasefire in occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast.[1] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Verkhovna Rada Deputy David Arakhamiya attended the ceremony alongside Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev and Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova. Lantratova is notably under US sanctions and has been directly implicated in the kidnapping of at least one Ukrainian child.[2] Dmitriev compared the Oleshky ceasefire to Melania Trump’s previous efforts to repatriate deported Ukrainian children from Russia.[3] Dmitriev highlighted the humanitarian success of the ceasefire without acknowledging that Russia’s invasion and occupation are entirely and solely responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky.[4] Dmitriev’s comments are in line with previous Russian efforts to use limited humanitarian cooperation — on crises like Oleshky or the return of forcibly deported Ukrainian children, for which Russia itself is uniquely responsible — to court the Trump Administration into adopting a more favorable posture toward Russia and to extract concessions from the United States in future negotiations.[5] Russian officials’ attempts to portray Russian President Vladimir Putin as a willing negotiator with humanitarian inclinations notably follow a string of devastating Russian strikes against Ukrainian civilians in recent months, including a recent strike that killed at least 14 people in Dnipro City while the Oleshky ceasefire was ongoing.[6]
The reported arrest of a prominent Russian milblogger for his coverage of the Oleshky ceasefire is likely part of long-standing Kremlin efforts to censor critical information space actors. Russian media and milbloggers reported on November 5 that Russian authorities arrested prominent Russian military correspondent Vladimir Romanov “Romanov Lite” in connection with his reporting on the humanitarian operation in occupied Oleshky.[7] Romanov reported on October 30, in a now altered post, that 17 buses with evacuated Oleshky residents would travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory and that four would go to Russia, but noted that Russian state media would likely show more buses going to Russia — implying that the Kremlin was planning to deliberately misreport on the humanitarian mission.[8] Romanov has not posted on his Telegram channel since October 31.[9] US outlet Newsmax, the only American outlet allowed into Oleshky, reported that 15 buses left Oleshky, with 11 bound for Ukraine and four to Russia.[10] The Kremlin engaged in a coordinated propaganda campaign intended to present the occupation of Oleshky in a way favorable to Russia in the lead-up to the occupation, and Romanov’s reporting directly undermined those Russian narrative curation efforts.[11] Romanov, one of the last outspoken Russian milbloggers, often criticizes the Russian military command for exaggerating Russian battlefield successes.[12] Russian authorities have long prosecuted and censored Russian milbloggers for speaking against the Kremlin’s false narratives of pervasive Russian battlefield successes, and Romanov’s arrest is likely part of the Kremlin’s efforts to restrict the Russian information space such that only approved pro-Kremlin media figures can retain a platform.[13]
Russia appears to be struggling to export diesel to the United States under the October 9 US-Russia diesel fuel agreement. The Financial Times reported on November 4 that the sanctioned Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leonean-flagged tanker Leruo , initially destined for the US, abruptly changed course on November 2, with the Talisman en route to Brazil while the Leruo steered away from the Atlantic Ocean into the Mediterranean Sea.[14] The Leruo is reportedly signaling “for orders,” indicating that the cargo does not have a confirmed buyer or destination port. Two other tankers carrying Russian diesel are still headed towards the US Atlantic Coast despite signaling that their cargo does not have an official destination port. The four tankers are currently operating without confirmed buyers, as Russia’s ability to successfully offload its diesel at a US port remains unclear. Russia itself is struggling with domestic diesel shortages, which is notable considering there are now four Russian diesel tankers floating in the ocean with no clear destination or buyer.[15] Ukraine’s intensified long-range strike campaign against Russian oil refineries has reduced Russia’s diesel supply domestically and its ability to supply diesel internationally.[16]
The Russian military is continuing the process of forming new maneuver divisions as part of longstanding plans to transition towards a force structure based on divisions and mass. A Russian milblogger published a recruitment advertisement on November 5 claiming that the Russian military command is reorganizing the 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade (3rd Combined Arms Army [CAA], formerly 2nd Luhansk People’s Republic Army Corps [LNR AC], Southern Military District [SMD]) into a division.[17] The reorganization of the 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade follows the recent reformation of the 4th Motorized Rifle Brigade (also of the 3rd CAA) into the 84th Motorized Rifle Division in early October 2026.[18] The 6th Brigade’s reformation, if confirmed, would mean that there are two division-level formations operating under the 3rd CAA, which is generally typical in the structure of a contemporary Russian CAA. The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) has not officially commented on the reorganization as of November 5. The 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade has been operating in the Kramatorsk direction, Donetsk Oblast.[19] The reorganization of the 4th Motorized Rifle Brigade and the 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade into divisions is part of ongoing military reforms that Former Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu announced in December 2022 and brings the total tally of Russian brigades reorganized into maneuver divisions to 13 since 2022.[20] It remains unclear if or how Russia will staff these formations to doctrinal end-strength.
Iran reportedly sought to acquire Russian military equipment in 2023 and 2024 that could support the regime’s counterinsurgency efforts. [NOTE: A version of the following text also appeared in ISW-CTP’s November 5 Iran Update.] Iran purchased at least six Mi-28 helicopters and at least 90 helicopter-mounted, APU-9L guided missile launchers from Russia in 2023 and Spring 2024, respectively, according to documents the Financial Times received from a Ukrainian private intelligence organization.[21] Iranian Deputy Defense and Armed Forces Logistics Minister Mehdi Farahi announced in November 2023 that Iran had “finalized” agreements to purchase at least six Russian Mi-28 helicopters, which can mount APU-9L launchers.[22] An Iranian journalist later shared footage of an Mi-28 in a hangar at an unspecified location in Tehran in January 2026, though it remains unclear whether Iran received the launchers and the guided missiles designated for the launchers.[23] APU-9L launchers are designed for Kh-39 LMUR guided missiles, and it is unclear whether they can accommodate other munitions.[24] The APU-9L system is designed for strikes against stationary and moving targets at ranges of up to 14.5 kilometers, meaning it can be deployed to strike force concentrations, radar stations, or electronic warfare assets, among others.[25] Iran likely sought to acquire these systems to support its counterinsurgency and border security operations, given the system’s limitations.

articles.title_orig: US Proposes New European Security Framework
articles.title_zh: US Proposes New European Security Framework
articles.content_orig:
In brief: US presidential adviser Jared Kushner outlined five objectives for a new European security framework ahead of trilateral peace negotiations with Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi next week. The proposal emphasizes crisis communications, military transparency, de-escalation and national sovereignty, while preserving NATO’s central role in European defense.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator Jared Kushner outlined five objectives for a broader European security framework on Thursday, Nov. 5, ahead of planned US-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi next week.
In a statement posted on X, Kushner said Trump had advanced discussions with several European leaders about establishing long-term security arrangements intended to prevent future conflicts.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The proposal follows negotiations in Brussels involving Ukraine, NATO, the European Union and other European partners.
“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Kushner wrote.
Kushner outlined five principal objectives:
Permanent security consultations.
Reliable crisis communications.
Greater military transparency.
Reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks.
A lasting framework for European security and stability.
He said Europe and Russia had struggled for more than three decades to establish sustainable security arrangements, with Russia’s war against Ukraine making the challenge more difficult.
The proposals aim to create mechanisms for regular communication, greater predictability and reducing the risk of future military confrontation.
Kushner emphasized that any future agreement must respect national sovereignty, territorial integrity and countries’ right to determine their own security arrangements.
“Each country will retain authority over its own security and alliances, and no country would have a veto over another’s sovereign choices,” he wrote.
The provision is particularly significant for Ukraine, whose ambitions to join NATO have long been opposed by Moscow.
Kushner also stressed that NATO would remain central to Europe’s collective defense and that the proposed framework would build on existing institutions rather than replace them.
The position contrasts with Russia’s longstanding demands that Ukraine abandon NATO membership ambitions and accept restrictions on its future security arrangements.
Kushner said consultations would continue through the Shell Bay format, involving Ukraine, NATO, the EU and European partners.
“We will also engage Russia as part of the peace negotiations,” he wrote.
The announcement comes ahead of US-mediated trilateral talks scheduled for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
As Kyiv Post reported , US envoy Steve Witkoff announced the negotiations earlier this week, saying they would address postwar security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures and steps toward ending the war.
Kushner said Washington would consult European governments throughout the process, with the possibility of expanding negotiations into a broader multilateral format if progress is achieved.
The proposed security framework remains under discussion, and no agreement has been announced.
The announcement follows a 90-minute conversation Wednesday between President Volodymyr Zelensky and US envoys Kushner and Witkoff.
As Kyiv Post reported , Zelensky said Ukraine had submitted its proposals to Washington and insisted that any postwar security guarantees must be binding and enforceable.
He also pressed the US for additional Patriot missile interceptors as Russia continues striking Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
Kushner acknowledged that the broader negotiations remain difficult but said Washington would continue working toward a comprehensive settlement.
“Creating the right structure will be critical to ending this war and transitioning from conflict toward conditions that make possible a durable peace,” he wrote.
It remains unclear how the proposed framework would accommodate Russia’s demands while upholding Ukraine’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to choose its own alliances.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.title_zh: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

Titled ‘Masters of our Destiny’, plan warns old trade relationship with US will not return
Canada unveiled a budget on Thursday that calls for “economic independence” and says that while reducing its reliance on the United States will take time, “the shift is under way”.
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s second budget since taking office last year was presented to parliament just two days after President Donald Trump suffered a sweeping midterm election rebuke.
While Democrats, who will take control of the US House and Senate next year, have already voiced a desire to ease Trump’s trade war with Canada, Carney’s budget affirms that the Canadian economy cannot remain dependent on the US market.

articles.title_orig: China offshore market is a value play amid the massive AI sell-off: CIO
articles.title_zh: China offshore market is a value play amid the massive AI sell-off: CIO
articles.content_orig:
The steep sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks likely has further to go, CNBC's Jim Cramer predicted Thursday — but he urged investors not to panic.
Growing opposition to new data centers following the midterm elections has raised doubts about future AI infrastructure spending, sending shares of companies tied to the buildout sharply lower. Micron tumbled 17%, GE Vernova dropped 7% and Sandisk plunged 22% on Thursday. All three stocks were also crushed in Wednesday's session.
"I wish I could say that today's flush was the bottom," the " Mad Money " host said, before cautioning that there may be more downside ahead, though he didn't believe this was an internet bubble redux. Cramer argued that today's AI companies are fundamentally different from the speculative businesses that collapsed during the dot-com bust.
"But I look at the charts, and there still seems like there's no support for so many Tech stocks, especially the semis, because they ran so much on the way up. However it might feel, it's actually an orderly decline because unlike 2000, these are mostly lucrative companies with stocks that went too high."
Investors had pushed AI stocks too high by assuming the rapid pace of data center construction would continue indefinitely, Cramer said. Smaller developers such as CoreWeave , Iren and Nebius face particular risks because they borrowed money to finance projects that could now face regulatory delays.
"That's what I am chiefly worried about," he said. "That's the real problem. That's what could really hurt the stock market. ... Right now, no one of significance is defaulting on their debt. The only issue with the debt is that it's connected to those neocloud companies that I mentioned. That's not enough to sink us."
Cramer suggested that a swift sell-off could help the market work off the excesses of the AI boom more effectively than a prolonged downturn.
"I for one am glad they are ripping the Band-Aid off this market rather than slowing trying to take it off a little bit each day," he said.
For investors, Cramer recommended maintaining sufficient cash. While semiconductor stocks could face further declines, he pointed to falling interest rates, signs of easing inflation and the possibility of an end to the Iran war as reasons for optimism.
"If you have cash you won't panic," Cramer concluded. "You won't be complacent, either. You will be clear-headed and that's how you will lose less money until things get better. They always do."

articles.title_orig: Trump says he and Putin are close to a deal about Ukraine and ‘all of Europe’
articles.title_zh: Trump says he and Putin are close to a deal about Ukraine and ‘all of Europe’
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday said a "very big" deal is in the works with Russia to end the Ukraine war.
Trump made the comments after he had an unscheduled meeting with Russian ⁠President Vladimir Putin's special envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House.
Speaking to ​reporters later, the president said the Russia-Ukraine war was ​very close to being settled and that bringing it to an end might involve "all of Europe."
"I can't tell you what I discussed. But I'm just telling you, it's going to be an agreement, it's going to be a big agreement," Trump said in the Oval Office.
"It's going to be very big. It's going to involve more than Ukraine , and I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."
Trump said he had not met with Ukrainian officials who were also at the White House on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Trump's son-in-law and US envoy Jared Kushner said the United States, NATO, ⁠and European ⁠partners held ​"productive and substantive ​discussions" on resolving ​the war in Ukraine Thursday.
"Our objective is to address the security concerns of all sides through practical, mutually agreed arrangements that reduce the risk of future conflict," he wrote on X, ​ahead of ⁠discussions ​next ​week in ​Abu Dhabi involving Kyiv and ​Moscow.
Even before his return to the White House, Trump has made similar promises regarding an imminent end to the conflict, famously saying he would end the war in one day upon becoming president.
Delegations from both Russia and Ukraine were at the White House on Thursday for an event honoring First Lady Melania Trump's work brokering a recent ceasefire in the war-ravaged city of Oleshky.
Speaking at her invitation, Russian envoy Dmitriev thanked the first lady for her "distinguished humanitarian role" in securing the six-day truce.
Dmitriev added that Putin personally gave instructions as part of the operation and sent his thanks to Melania Trump.
The head of the parliamentary faction of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's party, Davyd Arakhamia, and Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event.
Arakhamia told the first lady she did an "amazing job" and encouraged her to keep helping the Ukrainian people.
"Definitely we would like to ask you to keep going and to find new missions and to de-escalate more as much as possible," Arakhamia said.

articles.title_orig: Gulf Airports Built to Connect the World Are Now in the Crosshairs
articles.title_zh: Gulf Airports Built to Connect the World Are Now in the Crosshairs
articles.content_orig:
Resilience or luck? At the recent IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, this question was on every policymakerâs mind. There were good reasons for relief: despite a succession of shocks, the global economy had held up better than many feared. So too has the Middle East and North Africa.
When hostilities erupted in the Gulf at the end of February, provoking the largest oil and energy shock in history, many feared the regionâs economies would be overwhelmed: Shipping lanes would close, energy prices would soar, and the more vulnerable economies would struggle to stay afloat. Eight months later, those worst fears have not materialized. Activity has slowed sharply in some places, but it has not collapsed. In many economies, it has continued to expand.
Economies have adjusted, while existing buffers and policy responses have helped absorb the shock. But pressures are building, particularly in import-dependent, low-income, and fragile states.
The IMFâs latest Regional Economic Outlook for the Middle East and Central Asia projects output in the Middle East and North Africa to contract by 1.3% in 2026, 2.7 percentage points below our April forecast. Yet that headline figure conceals considerable differences in a region that spans more than 20 countries.
Several Gulf economies face deep contractions this year as disrupted energy production and trade take their toll. A sharp rebound is expected in 2027, assuming the conflict abates and trade gradually normalizes. But it will not erase the losses: Gulf output is projected to remain below pre-conflict expectations in the medium term.
Major oil importers like Egypt, Jordan, and Morocco have shown surprising resilience, with growth expected to exceed 4% this year. Remittances, tourism, investment, and favorable financial conditions have helped sustain growth, while policy measures have cushioned households from higher food and energy costs. But pressures are building, with inflation expected to decline more slowly than forecast in the spring.
The risks will grow the longer conflict-related disruptions persist. Low inventories and tight spare capacity could magnify further energy price spikes. Prolonged uncertainty could weigh on investment, tourism, and trade. The poorest economies are especially vulnerable: food accounts for a large share of household spending, and declining aid leaves less room to cushion another shock. A global market correction, whether prompted by a reassessment of AI-driven gains or interest rates remaining higher for longer, would add to the strain, particularly where financing needs are already large.
For MENA policymakers, the consensus in Bangkok was clear: In times of turbulence, preserving macroeconomic stability remains the immediate policy priority. As one finance minister put it, âthe policy frameworks and buffers built in good times decide how much room we have in the bad times.â
Policies should focus on containing inflation, preserving fiscal sustainability, and protecting the vulnerable. With food, energy, and transport costs rising, central banks need to guard against renewed inflation. Meanwhile, governments should protect vulnerable households while keeping debt manageable and pursuing the investment and reforms needed for future growth. That means mobilizing revenue, prioritizing spending, and ensuring support is targeted and temporary. Countries with stronger buffers have more room to support recovery and reconstruction. Those with less will face tougher choices to avoid adding to their debt.
But managing this shock is only part of the task. Regional economies need to prepare for the next crisis. Diversifying trade and production would reduce reliance on narrow export baskets and vulnerable transport routes. Better infrastructure and deeper regional integration would cut rerouting costs and strengthen supply chains. Investment in renewable energy would limit exposure to volatile fuel markets.
At the same time, the region needs new engines of growth. Digital technologies, including AI, offer opportunities as Gulf economies invest in data centers and digital infrastructure. Turning that investment into broader prosperity will require better education and skills, stronger governance and competition, and deeper links to global markets.
The experience of the past eight months suggests that resilience has been earned, through adjustment, stronger policy frameworks, and buffers built before the conflict. But resilience is a process. If the Middle East conflict persists and buffers are steadily depleted, todayâs delayed effects could become tomorrowâs larger adjustment.
Governments have an opportunity to act. In an era of recurring shocks, the economies that prepare before the next disruption will be best placed not just to endure it, but to emerge stronger.
Jihad Azour is the IMFâs Director for the Middle East and Central Asia Department

articles.title_orig: Retail traders dump $257 million in stocks in 5th biggest selling day since 2020
articles.title_zh: Retail traders dump $257 million in stocks in 5th biggest selling day since 2020
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Retail investors dumped US stocks on Thursday at a pace not seen since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, breaking with their typical market-down-day habit of "buying the dip."
Everyday investors sold a net $257 million in individual US stocks on Thursday, according to Vanda Research, the fifth biggest single-day of net selling spree since March 17, 2020, when retail investors pulled $502 million from individual stocks.
"This is what we would call a total capitulation by retail investors," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, said in emailed comments.
US stocks plunged on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5.2%, putting the index on track to close in a correction.
Retail selling marks something of a departure from a tendency by individual investors in recent years to scoop up shares when markets tumble. Vanda said there were "no signs of buying the dip" in individual stocks, though some investors continued to purchase leveraged exchange-traded funds such as ProShares UltraPro QQQ ( TQQQ ) and Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares ( SOXL ).
Vanda added that net selling was a third higher earlier Thursday afternoon before late "late-session" retail buyers stepped in
Patel added that the retreat echoed a broader "buyers' strike" among institutional investors alongside forced selling by systematic and leveraged investment strategies.

articles.title_orig: Stocks plunge as election outcome and AI worries crush tech shares
articles.title_zh: Stocks plunge as election outcome and AI worries crush tech shares
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Trump’s D.C.-area arch approved by federal planning commission as court battle looms
Stocks plummeted Thursday, as a blue wave of victories by anti-AI candidates from Maine to Alaska added to already growing fears about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped 6.3%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value, as investors stepped back to evaluate new risks to the billions of dollars in investments that have poured into the AI sector.
The S&P 500 plunged 4.4%, erasing $2.8 trillion from the index’s value. Both indexes suffered their worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, fell more than 5.5% and tumbled into “correction” territory, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%.
Markets had largely expected Democrats to win majorities in Congress. But they did not anticipate the scale of the victories, or the upset wins of candidates like Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, the largest data center market in the country.
Democrats still hope to clinch Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska. But already, hundreds of candidates who pledged to rein in AI data centers have been elected to office, raising the prospect of increased regulation on an industry that is the primary driver of U.S. economic growth.
Trump weighed in Thursday to blame the plummeting of stocks on Democrats.
“The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election. Such a sad thing to watch!” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social . “It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE.”
Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for AI’s development and operation.
Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq Composite is still up by more than 30%, despite recent fears that have sharply driven down chip, memory, and other AI- and cloud computing-linked stocks.
But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months.
“I don’t think this is an AI bubble bursting,” said Ed Yardeni, longtime market watcher and president of Yardeni Research. “I think it’s an AI bubble losing some air very, very rapidly, and I think that reduces the likelihood that we’ll get a bursting bubble that has adverse consequences for the economy and broader financial system.”
The selling continued as Asian markets opened on Friday morning local time. Korea’s Kospi index plunged 8%, triggering a market-wide trading halt. AI data center suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix fell by at least 9% in early trading.  Japan’s Nikkei 225 index tumbled 3%.
The commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections hit investors hard Thursday, after stocks initially rallied, on what many said was relief that the results of the midterms were projected quickly and clearly.
Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general and Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers.
Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets.
Democrats who won other state and federal offices have also voiced concerns about the industry and its companies.
“Today is the cold shower that I anticipated might occur after a blue-wave situation,” Yardeni said.
Elon Musk’s companies SpaceX and Tesla each slid nearly 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. But the two companies are also engaged in developing AI, and SpaceX has recently emerged as a data center developer.
On paper, both of Musk’s companies have shed more than $400 billion in value since Tuesday’s election results.
Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, spent hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories.
Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels.
The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed.
Arm Holdings slid 13%, while Qualcomm tumbled 9.5%.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index sold off by 12.3%, its worst day since March 2020, when the coronavirus pandemic began to shutter the economy. The “DRAM” ETF, which tracks firms that manufacture computer memory, sank almost 18%.
Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector.
SanDisk shares plummeted 22%, Micron, Western Digital and AMD fell 17%, while Seagate fell 16%. All of those firms were among the worst performing S&P 500 stocks.
Oil prices rebounded from Wednesday’s drop. Brent crude oil ended the day up by 3.8%. U.S. crude oil rose 2.7% on Thursday.
U.S. Treasury yields, which have faced some competition from tech giants tapping the bond markets to raise funds for their AI ambitions, were slightly lower.
In the wake of the market moves, traders dialed back bets that the Federal Reserve would raise rates during its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Odds are currently around 60%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,833 points or 3.4%. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold off by 9.2%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025.
Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months.
Major established cloud computing providers Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell, but less than the overall market declines.
Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 6%.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
Allie Canal is a business reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 more years in prison
articles.title_zh: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 more years in prison
articles.content_orig:
Joshua Wong, once a teenage figurehead of Hong Kong’s democracy movement, faces the prospect of entering middle age in prison, after a court Thursday meted out a 10-year sentence over a second national security conviction.
Wong became a prominent activist when he was a teenager, and entered prison for the first time at 23. He turned 30 last month.
In September, he pleaded guilty to conspiring with fellow activists to invite foreign sanctions against China and Hong Kong in 2020 – the year Beijing introduced the city’s National Security Law (NSL), which led to a crackdown on dissent, the shuttering of vocal news outlets, and the dissolution of civic groups.
Wong is already serving 4 years and 8 months in prison, after pleading guilty in a landmark subversion trial in 2024. He was due for release in January.
Beijing imposed the NSL on Hong Kong after huge and often violent pro-democracy protests convulsed the international financial hub in 2019.
The law tightened Beijing’s grip on the former British colony. Both the Hong Kong and Chinese governments say it has helped restore stability, but rights groups say the law has stifled dissent and made any criticism of the government risky.
Calling Wong’s case “grave,” Judge William Tam said the activist conspired with others – including Nathan Law, a former legislator now living in self-exile overseas – to call for foreign sanctions at a time when Hong Kong was dealing with its own social turmoil, referring to the anti-government protests.
After the NSL came in, the judge said, Wong and his conspirators “continued to promote such calls not only through their own social media accounts but also via prominent news media or outlets in the West, reaching both local and international audience.”
“Whilst it is a very heavy sentence on the defendant, the punishment must fit the gravity of the crime committed,” he said, adding that it’s “also necessary for this court to express the community’s abhorrence” at Wong’s actions.
In his mitigation letter, viewed by CNN, Wong wrote that his activism “was never driven by hatred.”
He’s been spending his spare time in jail studying the law and keeping abreast of technological advances, including artificial intelligence, he said.
“Yet none of my aspirations for the future is more important than my solemn wish to care for my ageing parents once I complete my sentence,” he wrote.
China’s leaders have previously labeled Wong and other activists “separatists.”
In the latest case, prosecutors accused Wong of conspiring with others to lobby the United States and other countries to sanction China and Hong Kong, prior to the NSL’s imposition.
This, they said, happened through social media campaigning, as well as meetings with US politicians, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and then Senator Marco Rubio, now the US secretary of state.
The lobbying continued after the law was enacted, prosecutors said, with the US sanctioning more than a dozen Hong Kong and Chinese officials after 2020.
A Hong Kong government spokesperson earlier dismissed international criticism of Wong’s prosecution.
“The lawful exercise of free speech must not be conflated with taking actions to collude with a foreign country to impose ‘sanctions’ to harm one’s own country,” they said in September.
Speaking after the sentence was announced, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, a former top security official, said Wong and Law committed “extremely serious offences, which not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society.”
Ahead of the sentencing Thursday morning, police had heightened security outside the court near Hong Kong’s financial district, where dozens of people had camped out – some for two nights – to catch a glimpse of one of the city’s most famous prisoners.
Among them was housewife ET Wong, who said she had started following Wong’s campaigning when he was still an adolescent.
“He chose a difficult path for the future, human rights and student movements of Hong Kong,” she said. “He should not have been in jail for one single day.”
Activist Lui Yuk-lin held a card with Wong’s name on it as she entered the building, lamenting the fate of the former teen figurehead.
“He’s a child in my heart,” she said.
When he was led into court, Wong, wearing a navy shirt and his usual black-framed glasses, nodded to supporters in the public gallery. Given the limited space, well-wishers took turns filing through the gallery.
Weeks after pleading guilty to his second national security charge in September, Wong – who’s been behind bars since 2020 – told his friend in a letter that he had been feeling “so-so.”
“[It’s] very difficult to describe the feeling and thought,” Wong wrote in the letter, shared with CNN by his friend.
But the former activist also encouraged his friend to stay positive, citing a verse from the Bible.
“There is no fear in love,” Wong wrote, quoting from The First Epistle of John, adding that the fear he had experienced over the past few years made him appreciate his love for his friends and the city even more.
Louis Lee, who shared his exchanges with Wong, said they discussed everything from music to their favourite Japanese anime, and would reminiscence about good times.
Reading Wong’s letters sometimes brought Lee to tears.
“As a friend, I miss him so much and I long to see the day when he’s out of the prison,” Lee said.
The skinny, bespectacled activist with a knack for fiery public speaking rose to prominence in 2012 at the age of 15, leading sit-in protests with his friends to successfully overturn a government plan to introduce Chinese civic education to the city’s schools.
At the time, critics feared the proposed curriculum amounted to propaganda by Beijing. Under the NSL, it’s now compulsory in every school.
Two years later, Wong became one of the key leaders of the city’s Umbrella Movement protests that rallied thousands of predominantly young people to the streets to call for greater democracy by blocking major thoroughfares for 79 straight days.
In 2016, he co-founded pro-democracy party Demosisto, which successfully sent co-founder Law to the city’s Legislative Council as its youngest member (Wong was too young to run.) The party announced its disbandment hours after Beijing passed the NSL, with Law revealing days later he had left Hong Kong.
Law is now one of dozens of democracy activists overseas wanted by Hong Kong’s national security police, and who have had a cash bounty put on them.
Authorities disqualified Wong when he tried to run again in 2020. He was later arrested and charged along with dozens of others for taking part in unofficial primaries held to screen candidates for Legislative Council elections.
In what was widely known as the “47 case,” after the number of opposition figures on trial, prosecutors said Wong and others subverted the Hong Kong government in 2020 by engaging in a primary election – a common practice in many democracies.
At the time, Hong Kong authorities said the primary vote was a “vicious plot” intended to “paralyze the government and undermine state power,” and accused those who took part of intending to use their mandate to block legislation indiscriminately.
Of the 47, most pleaded guilty while 14 were convicted and sentenced to up to 10 years in prison, after a 2024 trial that marked the single largest prosecution of pro-democracy activists under the NSL. Two were acquitted.
Since the NSL came into effect, civil groups have disbanded, and some independent media outlets have been shut down. The city’s legislature now comprises only pro-Beijing loyalists, while most pro-democracy figures are either in jail or in exile overseas.

articles.title_orig: China, DPRK reaffirm commitment to closer ties
articles.title_zh: China, DPRK reaffirm commitment to closer ties
articles.content_orig:
By ZHAO JIA | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-06 10:09
China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea have reaffirmed their commitment to deepening friendly ties and sharing experience in party governance, marking the latest in a series of high-level exchanges between the two neighbors.
The commitments were made on Thursday when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met in Beijing with a Workers' Party of Korea delegation led by Kim Song-nam, a member of the Political Bureau, secretary and international department director of the Central Committee of the WPK.
Wang, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, said China stands ready to work with the DPRK to implement the important consensus reached by the top leaders of the two parties and countries, deepen bilateral relations and deliver greater benefits to both peoples.
Close exchanges between President Xi Jinping, who is also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, and Kim Jong-un, general secretary of the WPK and president of the State Affairs of the DPRK, have guided the continued improvement of bilateral ties, Wang said.
In particular, he said Xi's state visit to the DPRK in June saw the two leaders reach a series of important common understandings, charting the course for bilateral relations in the new era.
Briefing the delegation on the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, Wang said the most important outcome was the adoption of the resolution on certain major issues concerning persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance.
The resolution carries major immediate significance and provides long-term guidance for strengthening the Party and advancing the building of a strong country and national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization, he said.
China stands ready to strengthen exchanges of experience and mutual learning with the DPRK on party and state governance to support the development of both parties and advance the socialist cause in both countries, he added.
Kim Song-nam said the deep friendship and strategic guidance of the two leaders form the fundamental cornerstone of China-DPRK friendship, while socialism is their shared ideal, banner and cause.
Pyongyang is willing to work with Beijing to make tireless efforts to advance China-DPRK friendly relations, he added.
Thursday's meeting came within two weeks after Kim Jong-un paid a visit to Dandong, Liaoning province.
Exchanges and cooperation between the two countries have deepened across various fields over the past two years. Bilateral trade in the first half of this year reached its highest level for the period since 2018.
International passenger train services, Air China flights and operations at land border crossings have all fully resumed this year. The New Yalu River Bridge, opened on Oct 15, is expected to further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges.
Yang Danzhi, a research fellow at the National Institute of International Strategy at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said deepening practical cooperation and exchanges on state governance and party building helps carry forward the revolutionary legacy and traditional friendship between the two parties and countries and opens a new chapter in China-DPRK relations.

articles.title_orig: Meeks launches bid to chair Foreign Affairs again
articles.title_zh: Meeks launches bid to chair Foreign Affairs again
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.
The letter, which officially announced his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.
Meeks and other Democrats have repeatedly forced votes this year on war powers resolutions seeking to end the Iran war, with a Meeks-sponsored one clearing both chambers of Congress.
But those resolutions have been nonbinding concurrent resolutions, since the 1973 War Powers Resolution only lays out a fast-track procedure the minority party can wield for concurrent resolutions in the House.
With a House majority, though, Democrats could bring binding joint resolutions to the floor.
Beyond war powers votes, Meeks also promised public hearings on the war. He also vowed hearings on a range of topics including the administration’s Venezuela policy and “repeated defiance of Congress’s constitutional authority over war powers and trade.”
“As chairman in the 120th Congress, oversight of this administration’s lawlessness and corruption will be at the top of the agenda,” Meeks wrote. “I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.”
In addition to Iran measures, Meeks also promised legislation focused on “clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy” and a State Department reauthorization bill that puts guardrails on the administration and protects career diplomats.
Meanwhile, the GOP side of the committee is poised to lose at least a dozen lawmakers — or about half of its members — next year between retirements and election losses.
The departures include longtime members such as former Chairman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who opted not to seek reelection, and Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., the Freedom Caucus chair who lost his reelection race.
Several other Republican committee members remained locked in races that were still too close to call as of Thursday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, potentially gutting the GOP committee bench further. They include GOP Rep. Young Kim of California, the East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee chair who was trailing her in race against fellow California Republican Rep. Ken Calvert.
Rep. Christopher H. Smith, R-N.J., who chairs the Africa Subcommittee, lamented the turnover Thursday but predicted a lot of interest among remaining House Republicans to fill the void.
“There will be many who will want to be on it,” Smith told reporters. “We lost some really great people. Yesterday I can’t tell you how sad I was about friends who are now not coming back.”
Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

The meltdown was broad across the major indexes, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite COMP bearing the brunt of the retreat, plunging 5.4%. The S&P 500 ( SP500 ) dropped 4.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJI declined 3.2%.
Just a day after logging one of its busiest trading days of the year—when markets rallied on the outcome of the midterm elections, which delivered a major victory for Democrats in both the Senate and the House of Representatives—Goldman Sachs’ equities desk observed a market suddenly devoid of buyers and dominated by top-down macro selling.
Long-only institutional investors remained frozen on the sidelines following heavy de-risking into midterms, while hedge funds actively offloaded hyperscaler MSFT AMZN GOOG GOOGL META holdings purchased just a day prior, Goldman partner John Flood wrote in an intraday note.
The wide selloff drove heavy volume spikes relative to 20-day averages—up 160% in the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF SPY , 150% in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF SMH , 100% in the Invesco QQQ Trust QQQ , and 75% in DRAM DRAM -related products—compounded by a second straight day of heavy retail selling skews, the note said. articles.title_orig: Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo
articles.title_zh: Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo
articles.content_orig:
While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.
The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.
As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”
He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”
The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:
The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo
Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.
The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.
For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:
sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0
To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:
sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode
Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.
To read Apple’s full support article, follow this link . And make sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the new MacBook Pro .
