articles.title_orig: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
articles.title_zh: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development.
Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide.
The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6% lower in early trading as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost over 12.6% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 9.5%.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%.
The sell-off in Seoul sent the Kospi index plunging more than 8.5%, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.
Taiwan's Taiex dropped by more than 8.3%, with chipmaking giant TSMC falling by nearly 8.5%.
It marks a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen.
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"
Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
In European trading on Thursday, shares in chipmaker Infineon fell by more than 8.5% while tech equipment manufacturer ASML dropped by 6.5%.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value in New York trading.
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.
The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.
The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Greater scrutiny of data centre approvals, and their impact on the environment and electricity bills could delay projects and raise costs across the industry, said Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist at Saxo.
While both political parties are keen to ensure the US' dominance in the technology, "there is a difference between supporting AI development and allowing infrastructure to expand at any cost or pace," she said.
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction .
With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

That is about four times colder than the previous best, set in a German drop tower, and colder than anything reached by Nasa’s Cold Atom Lab on the International Space Station (ISS). articles.title_orig: Grizzly bears may have attacked mother and daughter found dead in Canada
articles.title_zh: Grizzly bears may have attacked mother and daughter found dead in Canada
articles.content_orig:
Conservation officers say more than one bear may have been involved in attack on women near their home
Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre of the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service was investigating the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.
A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.
“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (5 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
The province’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, called the news “heartbreaking” and said he was thinking of the victims’ family and the Nuxalk Nation.
“At a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day.”

The results also included Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races and widespread support for local measures restricting data-centre developments.
Wall Street initially welcomed the outcome. On Wednesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.4%, as investors anticipated reduced political uncertainty.
However, that rally reversed sharply on Thursday as investors reassessed the implications of Democratic victories for the artificial intelligence industry.

The S&P 500 dropped 4.4% to 7,353.73, its steepest decline since the April 2025 tariff selloff. The Dow lost 1,833 points, or 3.4%, while the Nasdaq plunged 5.5%, its worst session in 18 months. The Russell 2000 also fell 4.4%.
The losses were concentrated in technology and semiconductor stocks amid concerns that Democratic lawmakers and newly elected governors could introduce tighter restrictions on data-centre construction, potentially slowing the expansion of AI infrastructure.
At least 38 jurisdictions passed restrictions or bans on data-centre projects, while Texas' incoming Democratic Governor Gina Hinojosa has advocated a moratorium on new developments.
Nvidia fell around 9%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 17% and Micron declined more than 17%.
The Nasdaq's market capitalisation shed about $2 trillion during Thursday's selloff, according to Reuters, as investors reassessed the growth outlook for AI infrastructure.
While the Dow's decline marked its worst second trading session following a midterm election in records dating back to 1896, Thursday's broader market losses were not unprecedented. The S&P 500's 4.4% decline was its largest since April 2025.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq sell-off batters Asian chip stocks as SK Hynix, Samsung, Softbank, TSMC tumble
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq sell-off batters Asian chip stocks as SK Hynix, Samsung, Softbank, TSMC tumble
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector.
The rout came as investors worried that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure.
In Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2%, while Tokyo Electron slid 7.3%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 11.6%.
Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.
In Taiwan, semiconductor stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with contract chipmaker TSMC sliding 9.6%. Electronics manufacturers Hon Hai Precision Industry , also known as Foxconn, and Foxconn Technology fell 9.4% and 9.1%, respectively, as the regional technology rout deepened.
China was also caught in the regional sell-off, with the tech-heavy STAR Market and the ChiNext Artificial Intelligence Index both tumbling more than 4%.
The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending. It closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%.
The sell-off in Asian equities has been exacerbated by investors unwinding positions, stop-loss selling and heightened volatility, Timothy Moe, chief Asia Pacific equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Friday. He added that potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect demand and profits for Asian AI hardware suppliers.
"If there's concern about the speed and magnitude of buildout in the U.S., then obviously that's going to put all that into question," he said. "The market's tendency is always to shoot first and ask questions later. I think that's exactly what's happening now."

articles.title_orig: Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost
articles.title_zh: Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost
articles.content_orig:
KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla.—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.
With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP.Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.
Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.
The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts, 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.
Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine, and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.
“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”
The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.
Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.
Blue Origin is developing a third stage for New Glenn called GS3 (creatively named Glenn Stage 3) to offer direct injection to geostationary orbit and Earth-escape trajectories. The third stage fits within an interstage, preserving the full fairing volume for customer payloads.
The stage can fly on both the smaller 7×2 variant (as in seven first stage engines and two second stage engines) of New Glenn as well as the larger 9×4 variant. According to Blue Origin, a GS3-equipped New Glenn 7×2 can carry 8 metric tons directly to geostationary orbit and 10 metric tons to translunar injection. Those figures increase to 14 tons and 20 tons, respectively, for the larger 9×4 variant.
As the rocket’s third stage, it needs to be light, Limp said. For this reason, the third stage is made mostly of composites, which are high-performing and lightweight. But there’s a problem with that.
The stage will be powered by the company’s BE-7 engine, already used by its lunar landers. This engine is optimized for in-space operations and uses liquid hydrogen and oxygen propellants. But hydrogen is the smallest atom and therefore leaky. With composites, thermal cycling and mechanical strain can cause cracking, exacerbating losses of molecular hydrogen.
Limp said the company was not sure a large composite tank, 5.5-meter diameter in this case, could be constructed that would contain hydrogen at high pressures.
The company recently had a breakthrough at Launch Site One in Texas, when it completed its first composite liquid hydrogen tanking test. During the test, the tank was pressurized to 100 percent of the maximum force expected during operation for 2.5 hours. It was even successfully tested at 150 percent of this maximum pressure for 10 minutes.
That gave the company confidence that a GS3 based on composite tanks was a concept that could go forward, and now the company is aiming for a debut in 2028 for a government customer.
“We have one customer signed up for cislunar space in 2028,” Limp said. “We are open for business.”

articles.title_orig: DOJ Launches ‘Super Intelligence’ Task Force Because Apparently We’re Still Doing This
articles.title_zh: DOJ Launches ‘Super Intelligence’ Task Force Because Apparently We’re Still Doing This
articles.content_orig:
The DOJ has established a Super Intelligence Task Force (DOJ-SITF) to combat the criminal misuse of advanced intelligence technology.
The task force will coordinate federal investigations, prosecution priorities and civil enforcement involving super intelligence.
The DOJ will merge its existing Artificial Intelligence Task Force into the new organization.
The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has created a new task force to address criminal threats involving super intelligence (SI), putting federal prosecutors and investigators at the center of America’s emerging technology strategy. The initiative will target foreign adversaries and domestic actors who exploit advanced systems for unlawful purposes.
The DOJ Super Intelligence Task Force (DOJ-SITF) will also coordinate with the White House’s Super Intelligence Force (SIF). Its mandate extends beyond enforcement to supporting American technological leadership and protecting domestic innovation.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss will serve as co-chairs. The department will bring together several law enforcement and legal divisions to oversee the initiative.
The task force will coordinate criminal investigations and civil enforcement involving SI across the Justice Department. Its members will also resolve overlaps between investigations handled by different DOJ divisions and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices.
Federal prosecutors may need to notify the task force before opening certain investigations. They must also provide notice before pursuing charges or finalizing resolutions in relevant cases, when requested.
DOJ LAUNCHES SUPER INTELLIGENCE TASK FORCE ⬇️ @POTUS Trump has made clear that “America stands at the forefront of a new technological revolution in intelligence,” and the Department will be a leader in safeguarding against malicious SI actors. “The SI Task Force at the… pic.twitter.com/u0aW2eXcLS
The DOJ-SITF will establish enforcement priorities focused on public safety and preventing technological misuse. It will also develop prosecution guidance for unlawful SI-related activities.
Its responsibilities include evaluating corporate compliance measures. The department wants companies to maintain strong internal controls that prevent advanced systems from being exploited.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department would work with SI Force Chair Jay Clayton. Their partnership aims to protect critical technologies from domestic and foreign threats.
Blanche also warned that authorities would pursue individuals who misuse SI against American taxpayers. That includes threats targeting critical infrastructure and national security.
The new initiative will absorb the DOJ’s existing Artificial Intelligence Task Force, announced by Attorney General Pam Bondi in January 2026. That body will no longer operate independently.
Its personnel, ongoing work, reporting responsibilities, and existing materials will transfer to the new organization. The consolidation places the department’s existing technology enforcement efforts under one structure.
The DOJ-SITF will also serve as the department’s primary contact for the SIF. It can coordinate with other federal departments and agencies when necessary.
The memorandum establishing the task force also gives it a role in shaping future policy. Through the Offices of Legal Policy and Legislative Affairs, members will advise on legislative and regulatory proposals.
The stated objective is to encourage domestic Super Intelligence development without imposing burdensome regulations. The department also wants to strengthen corporate oversight and deter unlawful applications.
Woodward described the initiative as part of the DOJ’s broader public safety mission. He said the task force would support technological progress while preventing its misuse.
Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss pointed to another responsibility. He said the department must use existing law enforcement powers to deter improper conduct and improve reporting on technological risks.
The task force brings criminal enforcement, national security oversight and technology policy under one umbrella. Its effectiveness will depend on how federal agencies identify emerging threats and respond to companies or individuals that cross legal boundaries.

articles.title_orig: Texas governor-elect says state will have laws to shield citizens from data centers
articles.title_zh: Texas governor-elect says state will have laws to shield citizens from data centers
articles.content_orig:
Data centres and AI are already becoming politically fraught topics in Australia. ( ABC News: Norman Hermant )
It's hard to imagine that someone was a bigger loser than the Republican Party in yesterday's US midterm "blue wave".
But somehow, things went even worse for the data centre industry.
When data centres were on the ballot, they overwhelmingly lost. There were about 41 different proposals put to voters in ten states, and all but one are on track for a loss for data centres.
An upset in the Texas governor's race saw Democrat Gina Hinojosa sail to victory. This puts Hinojosa, who has called for a ban on data centre construction, in charge of a state that currently has the biggest pipeline for data centre construction . If the ban is carried out, this will likely put a big dent in national construction.
Less directly but perhaps more consequentially, it's also cemented data centres as a politically toxic issue.
Five per cent of all political ads on TV mentioned data centres, and the majority of them were negative. It was an even bigger proportion in states that have become hot spots for data centre construction — the topic was covered in as many as 14 per cent of all political ads in Wisconsin .
An exit poll of voters conducted by NBC News found that three-quarters of voters oppose the construction of data centres in their community. More than 50 per cent of them said it was a crucial issue or major issue in their vote.
The Raging Grannies protest data centres and power hikes in North Carolina, US. ( ABC News: Bec Symons )
Admittedly, data centres weren't the biggest issue overall. Corruption, cost of living, immigration and the Iran War all rated higher. But to keep things in perspective, data centres were not a political issue just two years ago.
I mean this literally: I couldn't find an exit poll that even asked voters about data centres. Nor can I remember a time that a technology issue was so front and centre for voters. (It feels a bit like a cursed monkey's paw somewhere just put one, shrivelled finger down for those who were hoping more people would pay attention to AI.)
By the end of the 2026 midterm elections, data centres had become a bipartisan issue with candidates from both major parties opposing their construction.
(As always, US President Donald Trump was iconoclastic in his increasingly lonely but still vocal support for data centres and his rebranded "super intelligence".)
There will be a lot of ink spilled on what voters were actually rejecting in this data centre repudiation.
Was this motivated by environmental concerns? NIMBYism? The industry's significant contribution to inflation? Is the opposition to data centres a proxy for opposition to AI — obviously intrinsically intertwined as its physical manifest — or the impact of big tech itself?
More broadly, was this white collar voters experiencing a new type of economic anxiety because they fear their roles could be automated using data centres?
It's obviously some combination of the above, but the proportions will matter a lot.
One group keenly watching this result is Australia's political class.
It's not surprising that people who walk the halls of parliament are political sickos like many of us, but they're also certainly taking note of the data centre issue with an eye to what it means for us, here.
We should heed a note of caution against trying to directly transplant the midterm results to our political environment.
Australia is not America in a lot of ways, including when it comes to data centres. We've definitely seen an explosion in construction and proposals for a new generation of bigger, hungrier data centres , but the scale of our build out pales in comparison to our American friends.
The combined capacity of Australia's existing 163 data centres is about 1.6 gigawatts, according to Data Centres Australia. America has about 30 times that, at around 50 gigawatts of capacity, by one estimate .
Our biggest data centre, AirTrunk's MEL1 in western Melbourne, is ten times smaller than the known capacity of Elon Musk's monstrous Colossus 2 (which was reportedly powered for a while by gas turbines without environmental permits , thanks in part to the laxer rules in the land of the free — another difference between our contexts).
Nor is the opposition to data centres here quite at the level of the American backlash. Recent polling found that 44 per cent of Australians would oppose a data centre built near them — not a great number for the industry, but not quite like the 76 per cent of Americans in exit polls.
Another major difference? Australia has a bipartisan consensus from the two major parties on data centres, but in the opposite direction.
Just last month, the chairs of the parliament's joint inquiry into AI — Labor's Jo Briskey and the Liberal's deputy chair Jonathon Duniam — took the unusual step of sending a letter mid-way through the inquiry's investigation to give an "early indicator" of what they'd found.
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam and Labor MP Jo Briskey are co-chairs the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
It outlined several things that would be required to get the top AI companies doing their "training" here — a goal that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also explicitly stated is an objective of his government.
Translation: Australia wants AI companies to build big data centres here.
Now, the Australian politicians, staffers and those in the data centre industry who I spoke to about the midterms aren't completely terrified by the result.
They're very aware of the existing political stigma around data centres. Many of them expect that this result, even though it's in a different context, will embolden anti-data centre organisers, who are already fresh off a few wins in the last few weeks.
But there is a sense that it's possible to avoid this kind of response if we can thread the needle of attracting AI investment — again, this means building data centres — if we do it on, in their words, "our terms".
This is the motivation behind the government's proposed new rules for data centres that are expected to be released by the end of the year.
There are proposals for data centres in many places across Australia. This artist's impression shows one proposed for near Wagga Wagga, NSW. ( Supplied: CDC Data Centres )
There is one other interesting downstream impact of a cooling data centre industry in the US.
With an American data centre slowdown, the computing crunch on major AI companies who are already fighting amongst themselves for resources will get even worse. This means there's even more pressure to look outside of the US. And guess which country is high up on many of the top AI companies' wish lists?
Australia is in a small group of dream destinations for major AI companies, and our leverage just grew. This could mean we can negotiate more from a tech industry increasingly desperate for a new place to call home: more money, stricter rules, a greater say over how they run — it's all on the table.
That must be an enticing thought for politicians already banking on extract concessions from these companies to piggyback our own AI industry and to jump-start our economy.
But there's probably another question itching at the back of their minds: Is this febrile feeling by the electorate towards data centres a cautionary tale that we can avoid? Or if our government's goal to lure major AI companies down here comes true, is it our political destiny?

articles.title_orig: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.title_zh: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
articles.content_orig:
Archaeologists have found the earliest evidence of people consuming cannabis for psychoactive purposes in a tomb dating back almost 3,000 years, according to a new study.
Researchers found preserved cannabis seeds and human hair at the monumental elite tomb in southern Siberia , lead study author Gino Caspari, a researcher at the University of Bern, Switzerland, told CNN.
“There is a lot of speculation about prehistoric use of plant-based drugs, but through this find we are actually able to show that there is a basis to it,” he said.
The tomb is located in the Uyuk Valley and contains the remains of various high-status individuals. Caspari and colleagues have been working there since 2017, uncovering evidence that the tomb dated from 2,800 years ago, during the earliest Scythian period.
“These were nomadic horse-back riders known for their skill of shooting from horseback and for their exquisite gold items,” he said.
At the site, Caspari and his colleagues spotted small black dots in the tomb and were able to identify them as cannabis seeds. They eventually recovered more than 1,400 of them and used radiocarbon dating to ascertain that they had been deposited around 2,800 years ago.
They also found preserved human hair, which they tested using a mass spectrometer.
“Surviving plant remains which are almost 3,000 years old are extremely rare,” Caspari told CNN, as they are generally poorly preserved.
“It is even rarer to find them in combination with human soft tissue like hair, which essentially allows (us) to drug test a person who has been dead for three millennia.”
Analysis revealed that the hair tested positive for THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol), the primary psychoactive compound in cannabis, as well as cannabinol, a chemical compound produced when THC is exposed to air.
“That was just an amazing moment,” said Caspari, who said that the discovery adds to our understanding of the history of the consumption of cannabis.
Up to now, scientists had found evidence that cannabis was cultivated in East Asia at least 6,000 years ago, probably for its oil-rich seeds, according to a statement from the researchers.
Evidence of the plant’s use for its mind-altering effects had previously been found as far back as 2,500 years ago, including in ritual practices in Central Asia, the statement adds.
“The cannabis use has to be seen in a ritual context in the tomb and may be connected to shamanistic beliefs,” Caspari told CNN.
“Since we have dozens of sacrificed horses and some potential human sacrifices it might also have been used to sedate the victims before something bad happened to them — but we cannot prove that,” he said.
“Surprisingly little is known about the deep time cultural history of this important crop. For example, we are not even sure what truly wild cannabis actually looks like,” he added.
“Now we have at least 3,000 years of psychoactive cannabis consumption on the Eurasian continent and it seems that at this point it was already spread from China to Europe,” he said.
“We think this provides a cultural anchor point for current debates on legalization and medical use of the plant.”
Caspari added that the team are now sequencing the ancient DNA of the seeds they found at the site.
“Having well-preserved plant DNA is even rarer than having plant remains and this is the oldest preserved cannabis DNA,” he said.
“In the next few years our team will probably rewrite part of the domestication history of cannabis.”
Roger Forshaw, an honorary lecturer in biomedical Egyptology at the University of Manchester, England, who was not involved in the study, told CNN that the research “provides some fascinating insights into the use of cannabis among early Iron Age communities in Central Asia, a practice for which direct archaeological evidence has previously been scarce.”
A mystery skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally have an identity
The fact that chemical traces of cannabis were found in the hair “provides direct molecular evidence of cannabis use and supports the interpretation that it formed part of the funerary rituals,” he said.
“Although we cannot be certain how the plant was administered or precisely what role it played in the burial rituals, the discovery adds considerably to our understanding of the use of psychoactive plants in ancient societies,” Forshaw added.
The study was published Thursday in the journal Science .

articles.title_orig: Marine Corps Declares It Needs Nine More Amphibious Warships To Carry Out Its Missions
articles.title_zh: Marine Corps Declares It Needs Nine More Amphibious Warships To Carry Out Its Missions
articles.content_orig:
Navy and Marine Corps leaders have recently come to the agreement that the Corps needs 40 amphibious ships to meet its goal of keeping three Marine Expeditionary Units (MEU) deployed at the same time. However, at the moment, the Navy has only 31 of these vessels, a minimum mandated by Congress, and now an effort is underway to convince lawmakers to increase the fleet.
MEUs, made up of about 2,200 Marines, are typically embarked on Amphibious Ready Groups (ARGs), which usually consist of an assault ship, two transport docks or dock landing ships. Support vessels, surface combatants and in some cases a nuclear fast attack submarine can make up the larger Expeditionary Strike Group.
Marine Corps Commandant Gen. Eric Smith’s top priority is meeting what is called the 3.0 ARG/MEU presence, said Shon Brodie, director of Maritime Expeditionary Warfare at the Corps’ Combat Development and Integration (CD&I) Directorate tasked with modernizing the Marines.
Smith “believes that the best thing that we as a service can do for the nation is provide the highly trained Marine Expeditionary Units, one from the East Coast, one from the West Coast, and that one in Japan, persistently,” Brodie told a small group of reporters, including from TWZ , on Wednesday.
To ensure that happens, Vice Chief of Naval Operations (VCNO) Adm. James W. Kilby and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps (ACMC) Gen. Bradford J. Gering “have worked really close together to try to understand the number of ships it would require to achieve 3.0 based on current readiness,” Brodie noted.
“The two analytical arms of both services have come to the conclusion that it takes 40 ships. That’s 13 big decks and 27 LPDs,” the Maritime Expeditionary Warfare director explained.
Big decks are the Navy’s Wasp class (LHD) and America class (LHA) amphibious assault ships. Their embarked Aviation Combat Elements (ACEs) can include F-35B Joint Strike Fighters , MV-22 tiltrotor aircraft , UH-1 , AH-1 and CH-53 helicopters , as well as Navy Seahawk helicopters . The LPDs are smaller [ Amphibious Transport Dock ships ], which also embark MV-22s and helicopters.
The capabilities of MEUs have grown over the past decade, allowing them, in limited cases, to take on tasks that once required an aircraft carrier strike group. MV-22 tiltrotors, and, more recently, F-35Bs, which can be embarked in large numbers in the so-called “Lightning carrier” configuration, have boosted the utility of these fighting units.
The amphibious ship requirements, which had been in discussion for a while, were finally hammered out over the past few months by the new Amphibious Force Readiness Board (AFRB), stated Brodie. The AFRB is a joint Navy-Marine Corps effort created to better track the readiness of the amphibious fleet , which has been a huge issue as we have frequently noted .
“Right now, I have 31 amphibious warfare ships,” stated Brodie. The biggest need at the moment, he added, is for additional amphibious assault ships.
The law calls for the service to have 10, but currently it has only nine. That’s because the USS Bonhomme Richard (LHD-6) was sent to the scrapyard in 2021 after being ravaged by a fire in 2020 .
Brodie said the Marines want to increase the number of mandated amphibious assault ships from 10 to 13.
“When I have a problem generating this force, it really revolves around the big deck,” he stated.
The call for a fleet of 40 amphibious ships, and especially 13 big decks, is a sharp departure from the guidance former Commandant Gen. David Berger introduced in 2019 that led to his Force Design 2030 plan . In these documents, Berger called for fewer amphibious assault ships and more smaller vessels . Berger was concerned about the growing array of threats to these large, slow-moving vessels from anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, and that was before one-way attack drones became such ubiquitous weapons of war. This strategy was seen as better suited for fighting in the Pacific in a modern context, not large scale beach landings of the past.
He also wanted to return the Corps to its naval roots ; small, dispersed stand-in forces working inside an adversary’s weapons engagement zone after two decades of ground pounding in Afghanistan and Iraq.
Given how much of a sea-change this new plan represents, reaching a 40 amphibious ship fleet that includes 13 big decks is no small task.
“I’ve got a sheet sitting right here in front of me that tells me how we get there,” Brodie added. “You can’t get there tomorrow, right? The only way for me to realistically increase that inventory is for me to build new ships and do a service-life extension on some of the selective ships that I currently have in the inventory.”
Brodie said that Kilby and Gering are going to approach Congress later this month to convey the need for more ships.
There is no set timeline to reach the 40-ship goal, the Marines told TWZ .
“We will have to await future congressional funding for these,” Lt. Col. Eric D. Flanagan, a USMC spokesman, told us, adding that there is a multi-ship procurement contract underway for several amphibious vessels. He was referring to HII being awarded a $9.6 billion multi-ship procurement contract in 2024 for the construction of three San Antonio class amphibious ships and a contract modification for the next America class large-deck amphibious ship.
“This combined procurement — the first of its kind for amphibious ships — begins the journey for the construction of LPDs 33, 34, 35 and LHA 10 for the U.S. Navy,” HII stated at the time .
The request for additional shipbuilding funds will likely face far stiffer headwinds now that the Democrats have won control of both the Senate and the House.
While the Trump administration continues to pursue a roughly $1.5 trillion defense budget for Fiscal Year 2027, which includes some $350 billion that would come from outside normal defense spending streams via the reconciliation process , a letter leaked yesterday from a top Democrat offers a glimpse into the challenges the new amphibious ship plan may face.
The letter from Rep. Adam Smith, a Washington state Democrat who is in line to become chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, makes clear that many programs and policy issues, as well as defense spending writ large, are set to be put under the microscope when the Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.
“We must thoroughly review our national defense strategy and develop a more realistic and sustainable approach that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or paid for through draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Smith wrote in his ‘dear colleagues’ letter.
All of this comes at a time when the Navy has been struggling to meet operational demands for surface combatants with its existing fleet. This has been further exacerbated by shakeups in separate plans to acquire new frigates and larger uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), as well as rising costs associated with its workhorse Arleigh Burke class destroyers .
On top of everything, conflicts in the Middle East have taken a toll on the Navy, incurring costs that need to be paid for.
In August, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle estimated as a result of the Operation Epic Fury fight against Iran, the Navy needed between $6 billion and $8 billion more than what was budgeted for in the 2026 fiscal year “to be whole and solvent for [Fiscal Year] 26,” Navy Times reported .
Overall, the U.S. military “has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July,” according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters last month .
In addition to not having enough ships to fulfill the mission, there is a big problem keeping the existing ones available. The Navy’s amphibious ship fleet had just a 47% combat surge readiness rate as of April, according to Kilby’s Fiscal Year 2027 budget request statement . As we have pointed out pr

articles.title_zh: Memory Stocks Are Tanking. Should You Buy the Dip?
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
You don't have to look that far to grasp the severity of the increasingly painful chip stock sell-off .
Just start with the two names that were (keyword: were) the leaders of the AI-fueled momentum for much of 2026: Sandisk ( SNDK ) and Micron ( MU ).
Micron stock crashed 14% on Thursday, bringing its one-month plunge to a startling 36%.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down an almost laughable 4.8 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.
Sandisk is in the same valuation boat as Micron, trading at about 4.9 times estimated forward earnings on a P/E basis. Similar to Sandisk, its business has been very strong, and the Street remains bullish on its profit outlook.
Sandisk stock is down 19% today, bringing its one-month drop to 29%.
For perspective here, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) trades at about 18.5 times estimated forward earnings.
The bottom line appears to be this: The market couldn't care less about the valuations on either former AI momentum darling. The prevailing view is that, with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate and victories in key governor races, the construction of new data centers will be slowed.
That could mean fewer orders for Micron and Sandisk and a reassessment of their longer-term earnings power.
In other words, each is likely a value trap — until the dust settles on the AI trade.

IonQ stock has dropped 32% in a month to $29.70, despite posting record Q2 revenue of $80 million, up 287% year over year.
Rigetti fell 28% and D-Wave dropped 35% over the same period, signaling a broad quantum sector selloff rather than an IonQ-specific problem.
IonQ's $1.9 billion GAAP net loss and $1.8 billion SkyWater acquisition create integration risk that could pressure margins heading into Q3 results on November 5.

Quantum computing stocks have spent the past month giving back ground, and IonQ ( NYSE:IONQ ) sits near the center of the slide. IonQ stock is down 32% over the past month, recently trading at $29.70. Shares are up 5% from the prior close, a modest bounce after a steep decline.
The selloff has hit the whole group, which suggests IonQ is moving with its sector as risk appetite for speculative technology cools off. Rigetti Computing ( NASDAQ:RGTI ) stock is down 28% over the past month to $10.94. Meanwhile, D-Wave Quantum ( NASDAQ:QBTS ) shares have slid 35% over the past month to $10.23, a steeper fall than IonQ's.
For IonQ, the pullback has come even after a strong second quarter and a string of acquisitions, leaving investors to figure out whether the slide points to lasting problems at IonQ or a correction across the whole sector.
IonQ's Q2 2026 revenue rose 287% year over year to a record $80.1 million in results released on August 5. Excluding acquisitions, IonQ grew 132% organically. CEO Niccolo de Masi spoke on the earnings call. He said that "Q2 2026 is the strongest quarter in IonQ's history and our fifth consecutive quarter of record results."

Management's 2026 revenue outlook for IonQ now includes the SkyWater Technology acquisition, which closed July 31, and calls for $450 million to $460 million. That $1.8 billion deal brought a semiconductor foundry in-house. On the hardware side, IonQ is developing its 256-qubit Superion system, and management plans to start commissioning those systems in 2027.
In September, IonQ announced a quantum computing partnership with NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ). A pending acquisition of Elisity would add to IonQ's quantum security business.
Wall Street remains mostly bullish on IonQ, with 11 Buy ratings and one Hold over the past three months. The average analyst price target on IonQ stands at $65.45.
IonQ's Q2 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) came in at negative $120.3 million, and its operating expenses reached $417.3 million. Under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), IonQ's net loss hit $1.9 billion, mostly because of a $1.6 billion non-cash warrant revaluation the company disclosed.
All the acquisitions make IonQ's organic growth harder to judge. Folding in SkyWater could also put pressure on IonQ's margins. On the August call, IonQ CFO Inder Singh said, "So don't draw a straight line up into the right from any one of the data points."
The commercial return for IonQ still depends on how well it executes and how fast customers adopt quantum tools. Quantum stocks have also been volatile. As the past month's drops at Rigetti and D-Wave show, that volatility is exactly why speculative names like these belong in a small, rules-based allocation of a portfolio (we laid out the sizing and exit rules in a free guide here).
IonQ builds trapped-ion quantum computers and sells a full platform covering computing, networking, sensing and security, while Rigetti uses superconducting qubits at a smaller scale and D-Wave works on quantum annealing, which suits a different class of problems.
With SkyWater and Nexus Photonics, IonQ now handles chip manufacturing and integrated photonics itself, a vertically integrated model its two peers don't share.
Q3 2026 results from IonQ arrive on November 5, after the market close. Analysts expect a loss of $0.34 per share, compared with a $3.58 loss a year earlier. Investors will be watching whether organic revenue keeps growing apart from acquired sales and whether SkyWater weighs on margins.
Bulls have record revenue, a bigger outlook and an active hardware roadmap on their side. IonQ's bears point to deep losses, heavy spending and a sector subject to sharp swings. Whether IonQ looks hopeless or ready for a rebound depends on which of those lists the coming quarters back up.
Investors can watch for updates on the Superion timeline and on SkyWater's margins in the upcoming report. Cautious traders may want to see how the debate over IonQ's margins settles before drawing any firm conclusions.

articles.title_orig: IRS adjusts 2027 tax brackets. How your paycheck changes
articles.title_zh: IRS adjusts 2027 tax brackets. How your paycheck changes
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

articles.title_orig: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later.
The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market.
Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022.
Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months.
The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later.
The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development.
Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade.
Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well.
The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974.
"The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said.
Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.
Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
— CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report

The IRS has released the 2027 standard deduction amounts you'll use for your 2027 tax return — and they're higher than ever.
The federal tax agency adjusts these amounts for each filing status every year. Since these adjustments are based on inflation, the standard deduction is higher for 2027 than in recent years.
Knowing the standard deduction for your status can help you determine whether you should plan to itemize or claim the standard deduction next year.

Taxpayers age 65 and older, as well as those who are blind, can claim an additional standard deduction . For 2027, that additional amount is $1,700 ($2,100 if unmarried and not a surviving spouse).
Those eligible can add the extra standard deduction to the regular amount for their filing status. A single taxpayer 65 or older (or who is blind) can claim a total standard deduction of $18,700 on their 2027 federal tax return.
Additionally, as Kiplinger has reported, the 2025 Trump tax bill introduced a new bonus standard deduction of $6,000 for those age 65 and older.
This can be added to the 2027 standard deduction for each eligible individual and can be claimed by those who itemize.
However, the "bonus" amount is temporary and phases out for incomes above certain thresholds.
Your standard deduction amount might differ if you can be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer’s federal tax return.
The 2027 standard deduction for dependents is limited to either $1,400 or the sum of $500 and the dependent's earned income, whichever is greater.
Note: The standard deduction for dependents cannot exceed the regular standard deduction for your filing status, even if your earned income is higher than the basic standard deduction amount.
Given the new senior bonus deduction, the existing extra standard deduction for those over age 65, and changes to the base standard deduction, the highest possible 2027 standard deduction amount is a whopping $48,600.
That amount is for married couples filing jointly who are both age 65 or older, qualify for the bonus deduction, and can claim the extra standard deduction for both spouses.
For more information on how to calculate your total standard deduction, see: The Extra Standard Deduction for People Age 65 and Older .

articles.title_orig: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.title_zh: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.content_orig:
The EU said on Thursday it was not yet clear whether a spate of hoax bomb alerts targeting European flights were connected and that it was following events closely with national authorities.
"Any threats against civilians are unacceptable," EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas posted on X, adding that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked."
The statement from Brussels comes after Italian, French and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled as at least 27 European flights were hit by hoax bomb alerts for the third day this week, authorities and airlines said.
The hoaxes particularly targeted low-cost carriers and flights to or from Bulgaria, Czech Republic and Italy.
Italian air force jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome while French fighters guided a Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight to a military base outside Paris. Bulgaria's air force escorted three planes targeted by threats.
Three flights were diverted in all but all the jets landed safely with no explosives found.
More than 20 hoaxes have now been reported this week with low-cost carrier Ryanair the victim of at least seven.
Three Ryanair planes headed for Sofia from Madrid, Copenhagen, and London Stansted were targeted by bomb threats, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport said.
Two of the planes landed in Sofia but the flight from London-Stansted was diverted to Plovdiv Airport, east of the capital.
Air force fighter jets escorted all three planes, the defence ministry said, saying such missions "detect, identify and escort the aircraft."
All three planes were later inspected, and no explosives were found, an interior ministry spokesperson told the AFP news agency.
A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and checked by bomb experts, a Rome Fiumicino Airport spokesperson told AFP.
A Finnair spokesperson Stiina Tuunanen, confirmed that "nothing unusual was found" when the jet landed.
Finnair has a “very clear process that we follow in situations like this and we always work closely with the local authorities," Tuunanen said.
She said another false bomb threat had targeted flight AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, without providing further information.
After receiving a threat, a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna, the airline said, "in accordance with established safety protocols and procedures".
Another Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed at its destination safely, "following which a crisis unit was set up at Henri Coanda Airport," the Romanian intelligence service said in a statement.
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was rerouted to France after a bomb threat. It was escorted by military aircraft to the Evreux air base west of Paris, French authorities said.
"The flight landed safely and Aer Lingus will work to reaccommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible,” the airline said in a statement.
Four Prague-bound planes flown by Ryanair, Easy Jet and Sky Express were also the target of threats.
"We perceive the credibility of the threats as low," said Czech police on X. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the situation and all necessary security measures have been activated."
Prague Airport spokeswoman Denisa Hejtmankova told AFP the airport had received all the threats in emails from anonymous addresses. It was not immediately clear which airlines were involved.
Two planes, meanwhile, that arrived at Copenhagen were also the object of threats.
"Our assessment is that there is no danger, and there has never been any danger, to passengers or anyone else at the airport," Copenhagen police told AFP.
The origin and motives of the threats were unknown, but come amid a rise in hybrid attacks in Europe, sometimes linked by authorities to Russia or Iran.
France's secretary general for defence and national security, Nicolas Roche, highlighted to parliament last month "the massing of hybrid attacks in all their diversity — sabotage, cyber, drones, espionage of course —that we are seeing take shape in Europe."
On Tuesday, 27 flights were targeted with bomb threats, all of which turned out to be hoaxes.
The alerts forced the closure of a Warsaw airport and the deployment of Italian air force jets to protect flights.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted due to a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to support Republican candidates, most to help Ken Paxton defeat Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race.
Talarico won. But it was the other Democrat upsets in the state, for governor and attorney general, that could cause bigger problems for Musk and his Texas-based companies: rocket and AI company SpaceX and electric car maker Tesla.
Not only will he likely face greater regulatory scrutiny, but both candidates took direct aim at Musk and his businesses while on the campaign trail.
“It’s less about the blue wave on the Senate or House side,” said tech analyst Daniel Ives, a SpaceX and Tesla bull, about what Tuesday’s election results mean for Musk. “It’s more with the Texas governor.”
Democrat Nathan Johnson, who is replacing Paxton as Texas attorney general, said in July that, if elected, he would investigate whether SpaceX’s Starlink service was unfairly awarded grants designed to expand rural broadband. The internet service is SpaceX’s most profitable unit.
And Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated incumbent Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers a major plank of her campaign. She has vowed to put a moratorium on new data center construction. Both Tesla and SpaceX have banked their future success on their AI efforts.
SpaceX is planning major investments in new data centers in the next year, including the massive Colossal 3 to be built just outside of Brownsville, Texas. Unlike a lot of artificial intelligence companies, SpaceX earns a profit from selling time on its servers and cloud platforms to other AI companies. Hinojosa’s proposed moratorium would be a critical blow to its plans.
“I mean, those Texas data center plans are a key part of Musk’s ambitions,” Ives said. He said that’s why SpaceX and Tesla shares fell Wednesday, both dropping more than 3%, even as many other tech stocks rose.
Musk, the world’s richest person with a net worth estimated at about $898 billion, likely won’t sweat the money he lost backing Republicans, or even Wednesday’s decline in value for his shares.
The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 midterm elections
The bigger issue for Musk is an increased level of scrutiny, which he noted on his social media platform, X, on Wednesday.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote, referencing his ultimate ambitions.
Experts say lifting and operating data centers in outer space still face many hurdles. But even if it was possible, SpaceX may have to take off from a spaceport in Louisiana if Texas moves to limit launches.
SpaceX has faced public criticism for the operation of its spaceport, “Starbase,” on Texas’ Gulf Coast. Some residents near the launch facilities have long expressed worries about disruptive sonic booms — which can be as loud as gunshots and register as small earthquakes — and collectively filed a lawsuit this year.
How AI companies spent money on the midterms
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. But Musk has previously downplayed sonic booms, saying in a 2022 post on X that “storms and hurricanes that are far more serious than Starship launches.”
Those resident complaints, however, could find a more sympathetic ear from Hinojosa compared to Abbott. (Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to questions from CNN about her position on the spaceport.)
Tesla also has a big operation in Texas, and its driverless “robotaxis” only operate in four cities in Texas and three cities in Florida. For comparison, rival Waymo, a unit of Alphabet, operates in 15 cities across the country.
Local governments decide which vehicles, self-driving or otherwise, are allowed on their roads.
Musk bankrolling group using AI to attack Talarico on AI
“It would it would be a big blow if robotaxis faced more regulation,” Ives said.
Tesla hasn’t listed profits or losses for its robotaxi service. But Musk has made it clear that Tesla’s future is selling rides in its robotaxis, not car sales. And a large part of Tesla’s evaluation is the expectation that its robotaxi service will eventually operate nationwide, Ives said.
Ives also says Hinojosa’s threat to the AI industry goes beyond just SpaceX. Texas is a key to US AI development. The state has the most planned data centers in the country, according to research firm Cleanview, and is second only to Virginia for the number open or under construction.
“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout which makes worries around the future of the datacenter buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” Ives said in a note to investors Wednesday. “SpaceX stock will be under pressure.”

articles.title_orig: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.title_zh: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.content_orig:
Organic sales fell 1.3%, including a 270 basis point headwind from the China social media disruption; the company kept its 2026 outlook
SOPA Images / Getty Images
Kimberly-Clark $KMB reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.70 a share from continuing operations on Thursday, up 17.2% from a year earlier, as a social media disruption in China weighed on sales.
Adjusted earnings topped the $1.65 a share that analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal . Net sales fell 0.4% to $4.1 billion, and organic sales declined 1.3%, including a headwind of about 270 basis points from the China disruption, the company said.
Adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark , which include discontinued operations, fell 6.6% to $1.70. Diluted earnings per share attributable to the company were $5.37, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. The latest quarter included a pre-tax gain of about $1.4 billion from the completion of its International Family Care and Professional business transaction with Suzano, which closed July 1.
In International Personal Care, organic sales fell 4.6%, including a headwind of about 770 basis points from China. Segment operating profit fell 32.7% to $144 million. North America organic sales rose 0.4%.
Adjusted operating profit was $677 million, down 0.9%, with the China disruption accounting for a headwind of about 530 basis points. Adjusted gross margin was 35.5%, down 130 basis points from a year earlier.
"Our third quarter results reflect a dynamic operating environment and several discrete impacts," Chairman and CEO Mike Hsu said in a statement.
In October, Chinese authorities said a multi-agency investigation found no formamide in the diapers it tested, including Kimberly-Clark ’s, and no health hazards from the claimed chemical, according to Reuters.
The company kept its 2026 outlook. It expects organic sales growth about 100 basis points below the 1.7% weighted average growth of its categories and countries, reflecting about 100 basis points of impact from the China disruptions. It expects adjusted operating profit to grow in the mid-single digits on a constant-currency basis. It expects adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations to grow in the high single digits, and adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark to decline in the low single digits, both on a constant-currency basis.
Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue, the maker of Tylenol, on Nov. 2. In October, the company had weighed a bond offering to help finance the Kenvue takeover , a deal valued at roughly $36 billion that included $6.7 billion in cash. JPMorgan $JPM Chase had supplied $7.7 billion of bridge financing for the transaction.

articles.title_orig: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.title_zh: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A San Diego-based franchisee of Outback Steakhouse filed for bankruptcy on Monday, citing expensive food and labor costs and declining customer traffic.
Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, which operates 61 Outback Steakhouse locations mostly in California, said it has been struggling since the COVID-19 pandemic . The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Wilmington, Del., seeking relief from hundreds of millions in debt.
Cerca Trova also operates Outback Steakhouses in Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico but said that California’s minimum wage laws have made labor especially pricey for a majority of its restaurants.
More than half the company’s employees work in California, according to court documents.
California’s minimum wage, effective at the start of this year, is $16.90 per hour. Fast-food employers must pay a higher minimum wage of $20 per hour, but Outback Steakhouse is not classified as a fast-food establishment under the law.
Beverly Hills-based Fat Brands Inc. said in a statement that it filed for bankruptcy on Monday to restructure the debt it accumulated while expanding its company portfolio, citing ‘difficult and largely unforeseen’ market conditions.
“By 2026, the pressures on the business had converged,” Cerca Trova Chief Executive David Goronkin said in a court filing. “Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise.”
The company’s debt has increased from $269 million in late 2020 to $449 million this year. It has between one and 49 creditors, court documents said.
Outback Steakhouse is not the only full-service casual dining restaurant to face challenges since the pandemic.
Red Lobster filed for bankruptcy in 2024, after its disastrous $20 all-you-can-eat shrimp deal . More recently, the Oprah-backed chain True Food Kitchen filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and closed three Southern California locations.
Inflation and economic pressure have led more Americans to eat at home or turn to fast food for a cheaper option, while the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic has curbed customers’ appetites.
The cost of beef has also been rising, up as much as 5% each year since 2022, Cerca Trova said in court filings.
Shares of Wendy’s jumped 15% at the opening bell after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the struggling burger chain
Cerca Trova was once the largest Outback Steakhouse franchisee, with 99 restaurants in 2018. As of June, there were 659 Outback Steakhouse locations nationwide, 544 owned and operated by the brand owner, Bloomin’ Brands. The rest are run by franchisees.
Bloomin’ Brands, headquartered in Tampa, Fla., also owns Bonefish Grill, Carrabba’s Italian Grill and Fleming’s Prime Steakhouse and Wine Bar.
The company has thrived this year despite pressures on the restaurant industry, with shares rising 60% since January. Shares fell Tuesday after Cerca Trova’s bankruptcy announcement and ended the day at $10.23, down 6.15%.  The company’s market value is nearly $879 million.
The Scottsdale, Ariz.-based health food chain True Food Kitchen announced it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Monday and has closed 12 locations.
Cerca Trova, also known as Out West Restaurant Group, proposed selling its assets to Bloomin’ Brands for $26.3 million unless a higher offer emerges during the bankruptcy process.
“This is an isolated situation involving the franchisee and does not affect Bloomin’ Brands’ corporate operations, financing, or liquidity,” Bloomin’ Brands spokesperson Elizabeth Daly said in an email. “Bloomin’ Brands is participating in the process as a stalking‑horse bidder to acquire Out West’s assets and seeking to support operational continuity and protect the brand while the court‑supervised process moves forward. ”
Cerca Trova could not be immediately reached for comment.

articles.title_orig: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.title_zh: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.content_orig:
The two companies helmed by the world's richest person have had a rough two-day stretch on the market. Tesla ( TSLA -10.77% ) closed at $398.50 on Election Day, and by 3:08 p.m. ET Thursday, it was trading at about $342, down 14%, representing a loss of about $225 billion in market value. SpaceX ( SPCX -9.05% ) fell from $141.31 to about $125, down 12%, or about $227 billion. Together, that's about $450 billion gone in two sessions, most of it on Thursday, when Tesla fell about 11% and SpaceX about 8%.
To illustrate how steep the drop has been, SpaceX is now trading below its $135 IPO price from June.
Image source: Getty Images.
If you had to sum it up in one word: politics. Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, and Musk, a top ally of President Donald Trump, is a likely target. Speaking on the All-In podcast on election night, Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz said Democrats had signaled they would use subpoenas "to go after Elon Musk." In Texas, home to both companies, voters elected a Democratic attorney general for the first time since 1994.
But political sentiment isn't the only reason. The Nasdaq was headed for its worst day in 18 months on Thursday as investors dumped chip and data-center stocks, on fears that new leaders in Washington and the states could slow data-center construction. SpaceX, of course, is exposed: Last month, it committed to a roughly $40 billion lease for AI chips with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, with payments starting in the first half of 2027.
Adding to the fire for SpaceX, Wall Street is reportedly trying to sell off pieces of that $40 billion chip deal to other investors, with Goldman Sachs and Apollo leading the effort, according to Bloomberg on Thursday.
SpaceX made money last quarter: $2.79 billion in operating income and $4.4 billion in net income, though it's still $413 million in the red for the first nine months of the year. Nothing that happened in Washington this week changes its launch business or Starlink.
But the fine print, or at least the filing details, are worth noting. That net income included a $390 million tax benefit and a $561 million unrealized gain on its stake in the Boring Company, Musk's tunneling firm, and two customers made up about half of quarterly revenue. Even after the drop, SpaceX is valued at about $1.7 trillion, roughly 150 times its third-quarter operating income on an annualized basis.
Part of Tesla's bull case rests on robotaxis. On Tesla's October earnings call , CFO Vaibhav Taneja told analysts he expects robotaxis to make a real dent in both sales and profits in 2027, and the firm said the Cybercab was due to launch in Dallas this month. Musk told analysts Tesla will end up doing "a majority of all passenger miles on earth" -- "unless we are stopped by governments."
That caveat matters more this week. Self-driving cars depend on regulators, and Washington just got less friendly to Musk. Taneja also conceded that the robotaxi business hasn't yet reached its cost target of 30 cents per mile.
The two companies are also tied together. Tesla's filing puts its SpaceX stake at $2.87 billion as of Sept. 30, and shows SpaceX with a $729 million balance owed to Tesla, most of it tied to Megapack batteries still on order. Bad news for one tends to hit the other.
Not all at once. The political risk is real, but for now it's mostly talk. The new Congress isn't seated until January, and investigations take time. Meanwhile, a two-day drop of 12% to 14% doesn't make either stock cheap.
If you believe in Musk's long-term plans, this is a reasonable time to start a position slowly. Buy in small pieces over several weeks, and keep it a small part of your portfolio, because these are among the most volatile tech stocks you can own.
If you can only pick one, SpaceX gives you a launch and satellite business that's already earning money, while much of Tesla's value rides on robotaxis that are just getting started. And if headlines out of Washington would keep you up at night, it's fine to wait until the political picture is clearer.
